name: Pacific Northwest coast
sow: Sow native seed outdoors in early autumn, September to October. Some species can also be sown in early spring (February to March), but they will usually need watering through their first summer.
why: Autumn sowing follows the natural cycle: seed ripens from spring to autumn, the winter rains water it in, and winter cold switches off the dormancy that many native seeds carry. Some species sprout in autumn; others wait until spring after a winter in the ground.

name: California lowlands
sow: Sow native wildflower seed from mid-October to November, just before or as the autumn rains begin. Sowing can continue through to January, and as late as March if you are prepared to water.
why: California's native annuals begin their yearly cycle with the autumn rains: seed germinates in the cool, wet months and flowers in spring. Sowing at this time copies nature and lets the rain do most of the watering.

name: Sonoran Desert, southern Arizona
sow: Sow spring-flowering desert wildflowers in autumn, from October to mid-December. Summer-flowering species that follow the monsoon are sown in spring instead.
why: Desert wildflower seed lies dormant through the hot, dry summer and germinates with the cool-season rains of autumn and winter. Seedlings stay small through winter and flower from February to April.
examples_label: Plants that sources say start readily from seed

examples.note: Blooms in spring and reseeds easily from year to year.

name: Tallgrass prairie and Upper Midwest
sow: Sow in late autumn as a dormant seeding, from about mid-October or early November until the ground freezes, so the seed lies outdoors over winter. Late spring (mid-May to 1 July in Minnesota) is the second window, but many wildflower seeds then need a cold, moist pre-treatment first.
why: Many prairie wildflower seeds need a period of cold, moist conditions before they will germinate, and a winter in the soil provides it naturally. A few species, such as wild bergamot, do not need the cold and can also be sown in spring.
examples_label: Plants that sources say start readily from seed

examples.note: Establishes reliably from seed and is found across Minnesota; the seed needs a cold, moist spell or an autumn sowing, and the plant is short-lived.
A widely distributed prairie plant that is easy to start from seed and does not need cold stratification.
Easy to grow and often flowers in its first year; the supplier lists a 30-day cold, moist treatment. A northern species, so check that it is native to your own area.

name: Northeastern North America
sow: Sow outdoors in pots from November to February and leave them out in the weather over winter. Seedlings appear in spring.
why: Many native seeds need a period of cold, moist conditions to break dormancy; sowing in autumn or winter lets the weather do this naturally.

name: Britain and Ireland
sow: Sow in early autumn (September) or in early to mid-spring (March and April). Yellow rattle is the exception: sow it fresh in August or September, and no later than November.
why: Most wildflowers shed their seed in late summer and autumn, and many need a cold winter to stimulate germination in spring. On heavy soil that stays wet and cold over winter, the RHS suggests waiting until spring.

examples.note: Easily grown from seed and germinates readily in both spring and autumn.

name: Central Europe
sow: Sow native wildflower seed in spring, from February or March to May, or in late summer and early autumn, from August to October. Choose a spell when lasting damp weather is expected.
why: Wildflower and wild grass seedlings need at least three weeks of unbroken moisture to swell and germinate. Some hard-coated seeds sown in autumn will not come up until the following spring.

name: Cape Floristic Region
sow: Sow Cape seed in autumn. Annuals are sown from early March and proteas from mid-March, as the days begin to cool.
why: Cape plants rest through the dry summer and begin growing again in autumn; annuals survive summer as seed and germinate with the autumn rains. Most Cape seeds also respond well to smoke treatment, even where they do not strictly need it.

name: Aotearoa New Zealand
sow: Sow native seed as soon as possible after collecting it, which for most species means late summer and autumn (February to May). Where young seedlings cannot be protected from frost, store the seed and sow in late winter (August) instead.
why: Most native seed ripens in late summer and autumn and is best sown fresh. Holding seed until late winter avoids frost damage to new seedlings.

examples.note: Easily raised in large numbers; the fine seed can be sprinkled on top of seed-raising mix, and it should be eco-sourced carefully because it varies across the country.

name: Japan
sow: Sow seed of native meadow plants gathered in autumn and early winter during the winter itself, so that it passes the cold season outdoors. Seed sown at another time first needs a cold spell in a refrigerator at about 5 °C.
why: Many native grassland plants that ripen seed in autumn and winter sprout the following spring, and their seed will not germinate until it has been exposed to a period of cold.
